name: Mentoring and Digital Wellbeing
title: Mentoring and Digital Wellbeing
answer: Mentoring and digital wellbeing is the practice of pairing students with supportive adults while also teaching students how to manage their own screen habits and emotions. AI can suggest mentor matches and draft social and emotional learning lessons, but the coordinator makes the final matches and the teacher adapts and checks every lesson. It matters because good matches and sound lessons depend on human understanding of the students involved, not on the tool that proposed them.

sections.body: This idea covers three connected pieces of school work: mentoring programs that connect students with adults who can support them, lessons that teach students about their own digital wellbeing, and social and emotional learning lessons. The problem it solves is capacity. A coordinator cannot easily scan every student's interests and needs against every available mentor, and teachers do not always have time to build lessons on screen time, social media, friendships, stress and emotions from scratch. AI features inside ordinary spreadsheets can suggest mentor matches, and tools such as MagicSchool can draft lesson plans, which gives staff a starting point rather than a finished product. The judgement about who should mentor whom, and what a class should actually be taught, stays with the people who know the students.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a mentoring program, the coordinator uses AI features in spreadsheets to suggest matches between students and adults based on interests and needs, then makes the final matches using what they know about both the students and the mentors. Teachers can lead lessons on screen time, social media and healthy habits without any special product, so this part of the work needs no new purchase. For social and emotional learning, a teacher might use MagicSchool to draft lessons on managing emotions, building friendships or handling stress, then adapts the lessons to their own students and checks that the content is sound. The text names middle school as the grade band in its survey of student internet use, and it does not assign the mentoring or lesson work to particular year groups. Across all of it, the lessons themselves are delivered by people who know the students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one piece of research for this idea and no evidence label beyond the citation itself. It reports that a survey of 3,378 middle school students in China found that more than three hours a day of entertainment internet use was linked to more anxiety and depression, while moderate gaming was not harmful (Li et al., 2023). That finding supports the case for teaching students about their own digital wellbeing. For the mentoring matches and the drafting of social and emotional learning lessons, the text gives no study, figure or finding, so those parts rest on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that the tool suggests and the person decides. The program coordinator makes the final mentor matches, using what they know about students and mentors, because a good match is built on human understanding. The teacher adapts drafted social and emotional learning lessons to their students and checks that the content is sound before it is used. The lessons themselves are delivered by people who know the students, not by the tool that drafted them. Nothing in the text removes these decisions from the adults responsible for the students.
